activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
story:
Avery spread two climate graphs across the library table and checked the clock on the wall. Forty minutes until her mom picked her up, and the project was due tomorrow. On the left, a rainforest graph from Brazil, its rainfall bars tall and crowded, some months topping 300 millimeters. On the right, her desert graph, copied from a book about the Atacama in Chile, and something about it was wrong.

Six of the twelve bars were missing. She counted again, pressing her finger to the paper. "I must have skipped them," she whispered. Her hand was hesitant as she picked up her pencil, because the paper cut on her knuckle had turned an angry red that morning and her mom had warned her about infection if she kept touching it. She decided to redraw the missing bars with reasonable guesses, maybe ten millimeters each, just to fill the space.

The library printer hummed behind her. She flipped back to the Atacama chapter and ran her finger down the data table, looking for the numbers she must have missed. The table listed weather stations down the side and years across the top. Station after station, column after column, empty. Not zero. Not small. Empty, with a dash where a number should be.

"That can't be right," she said out loud, and a boy at the next table glanced over. She gave him an awkward wave and pulled the atlas closer. Somewhere in the middle of the chapter she found one line, easy to skim past, and read it three times. Parts of the Atacama were so dry that some weather stations there had never recorded rain. Never. Not once, the whole time anyone had been measuring.

She looked at her guessed bars, each one a small lie sitting on the page. Slowly, she erased all six, the clock ticking toward pickup time. Then she drew a note in the margin: "No bars because no rain was ever recorded here." On her Brazil graph, one month showed 289 millimeters. She set the two pages side by side and stared at them until the difference felt almost impossible.

The boy leaned over on his way out. "You forgot half your bars," he said.

"I didn't forget anything," Avery said, and slid both graphs into her folder, the empty half facing up. "Some places just never got rained on."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
story:
Arthur had finished dead last in every eight-hundred-metre race since September, and today he intended to find out why. Coach Ruiz kept saying "pace yourself," which told him nothing, so he sat on the bleachers at Riverside Park with his training watch and a notebook, waiting for his friend Deshawn.

Deshawn jogged up the diagonal path from the parking lot, still wearing his spikes. He had won the race on Saturday, the same one where Arthur had faded badly on the second lap.

"I need your lap times," Arthur said. "Both laps. From Saturday."

Deshawn squinted at him. "Why?"

"Because something happens to me in the second lap, and I can't see it from inside my own head. Maybe the numbers can."

Deshawn pulled out his phone and read them off. First lap, sixty-two seconds. Second lap, fifty-eight. Arthur wrote them down, then looked at his own watch history. First lap, sixty-one. Second lap, seventy-one.

He stared at the two lines. Both of them had run the first lap fast, but only one of them had kept going. The difference wasn't speed at all. It was which half was faster.

"Wait," Arthur said. "You ran your second lap faster than your first. I did the opposite. Is there a word for that?"

"Yeah," Deshawn said. "A negative split. Second half faster. First half faster is a positive split."

"So the good one is negative?"

"The good one is negative," Deshawn confirmed, grinning.

Arthur felt a flicker of skepticism. It seemed too simple, a label for what went wrong. But a rule you could name was a rule you could test. He asked Deshawn to time him over two laps, with one instruction: go out slow on purpose, almost embarrassingly slow, and hold everything back until the bell sound of his watch at the halfway mark.

They set up at the far curve. Arthur went through the first lap in sixty-eight seconds, which felt like crawling, while Deshawn shouted splits from the fence. At the halfway mark Arthur pushed, and his legs, instead of turning to wood, actually responded. Second lap: sixty-five. Still slow overall, but faster than the first lap, and for the first time all season he crossed the finish line accelerating instead of dying.

He bent over, hands on knees, laughing at the grass.

Deshawn had originally wanted the track to himself that afternoon to work on his starts; that had been his whole plan. But he jogged over anyway, holding out the watch. "Do it again," he said. "This time I'll call out every two hundred."

Arthur straightened up, took a drink, and walked back to the start line. "Count me down from ten."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
story:
Isla knelt on the wooden bench beside the trail, the field microscope balanced on a flat rock between two tree roots. Her teacher had said anyone who drew a fully labeled onion cell sketch by the end of the hike would get to skip the worksheet, and Isla wanted that skip more than she wanted to admit. She had peeled a paper-thin layer of skin from the onion in her lunch, laid it on the slide, and now she squinted through the eyepiece at rows of neat rectangles, like bricks in a garden wall. The problem was the labels. She could see the cell wall easily, the rigid outer border of every brick, but the membrane hugging it inside was only a faint line, and the nucleus was nowhere at all.

Her friend Dev crouched next to her, hesitant to touch the precious slide. "Maybe you killed the cells when you peeled them," he said.

"They're onion skin. They were already dead-ish." She lifted her head and thought about the day last year when she'd nearly skipped the science museum trip to go to the arcade instead. Her mother had talked her into it, and it had turned out to be the museum that changed things. In a glass case there had been an enormous old drawing of tiny boxy shapes, crowded like a honeycomb, and a plaque beneath it. She remembered reading the plaque twice: Robert Hooke had named cells in his 1665 book, Micrographia, after seeing tiny compartments in a thin slice of cork under his microscope. She remembered it because the drawing had looked exactly like this, except his were empty boxes and hers had something inside them.

"Dev, Hooke saw compartments in cork. Empty ones, like dead rooms." She turned back to the eyepiece. "If the nucleus is missing, maybe it's invisible, not absent." She dug in the kit and found the small dropper bottle of iodine, the stain her teacher had mentioned only in passing. If staining worked, it would justify her whole theory; if it didn't, she'd wasted the slide and the afternoon.

She lifted the coverslip, let one amber drop soak into the skin, and waited, counting seconds while a crow argued somewhere up the trail. When she looked again, a dark dot sat near the center of each brick, round and unmistakable. "There," she said, stabbing her pencil at the paper. "Nucleus. Cell wall. And that thin inner line, that's the membrane." She drew the faint border carefully, thicker than life so her teacher could see it.

Dev leaned in to look. "You know the irony? Hooke looked at empty cork and got the name. You looked at the same shape and found what he couldn't." Isla printed her name at the top of the sketch and held it up against the light, one corner of her mouth lifting.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
story:
Peyton spread two stories side by side on the library table, one hers, one from her pen pal Kit in Manchester. The contest deadline was Friday, and she could not postpone it again, because she had already asked for one extension and the librarian, Ms. Okafor, had said no second chances. Both stories were due at nine in the morning, which meant tonight was the last night to fix them.

Kit's story came back covered in corrections, but the strangest ones were in the dialogue. Where Kit had written "Meet me at the lock," Peyton saw a red mark pulling the comma outside the closing quotation marks, the opposite of everything Peyton had learned. She stared at it, then at her own page, where every comma and period sat inside the quotes. One of them had to be wrong, and if it was hers, her contest entry was doomed.

Last summer, in the same library, she had formed a quiet alliance with a boy named Deshawn over the summer reading log, trading snacks for help with fractions. He was three tables away right now, hunched over a graphic novel. She carried both stories over and laid them in front of him. "Look at this," she said. "Same sentence, different punctuation. Which one is right?"

Deshawn squinted. "Yours looks right to me." He turned the pages. "Wait. Where's Kit from?"

"England. Manchester."

"That might be it," Deshawn said slowly. "British usage often puts the comma outside the quotation marks." He tapped Kit's page. "In American English it goes inside. So Kit's not wrong either. You're both right, just different rules."

Peyton tested it, because she did not want to believe it on one boy's word. She pulled the style guide from the reference shelf and found the rule printed in black and white, with examples, exactly as Deshawn had said. Then she found a British grammar site on the library computer and found the opposite rule stated just as firmly. It was like discovering that two countries drove on different sides of the same road, and neither one was crashing.

Her problem now was her own story. She had a scene where two friends argue about a stolen bike, but the ending was ambiguous; her teacher had written "unclear who wins" in the margin, and Peyton had ignored it for two weeks. If she cut the last argument short and let one friend say "I took it, and I'm sorry," with the period tucked inside the quotation marks, the climax would land in one clean line. She crossed out three paragraphs, wrote the new ending, and read it aloud in a whisper at the table.

"There," she said. "The confession is the climax. And every comma stays inside, American style." Deshawn gave her a thumbs-up without looking up from his graphic novel. Peyton printed the story, stapled it, and slid it into the contest box by the front desk just as the clock above the returns counter touched nine.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
story:
Theo's history teacher had taped a map of 1919 Europe to the classroom door, and next to it she had pinned a single question: "How did the Treaty of Versailles help lead to the Second World War?" Each student had to explain it out loud on Friday, and Theo had exactly nothing.

"I'm going to fail," he told Priya at lunch, poking at his tray of lasagna. "I can memorize dates, but this is a why question. You can't see a why."

Priya, who was eating an apple in neat proportional slices, one eighth at a time, shrugged. "Then stop trying to see it. Test it. Mr. Okafor says that all the time about science."

That gave Theo an idea. On his walk home he passed the war memorial in the square, the stone arch with names carved into it, and he stopped and stared at it. His grandfather's cousin was on that wall. He tried to picture Germany after the first war, and he realized he had been picturing it wrong, like a defeated team simply deciding to be strong again. That made no sense. Teams that lose get weaker, not stronger. Something had to limit Germany first, and then something had to break the limit.

At home he opened his textbook and hunted until he found it. The Treaty of Versailles, the peace signed after the First World War, had forced Germany to shrink its army to 100,000 soldiers and had banned Germany from having an air force at all. Theo read the line twice. A hundred thousand sounded big until he remembered that the whole point was that Germany later built a huge army again, with planes, only about twenty years later. So the treaty had created a cage, and somehow the cage got opened. That was the hidden cause he had been missing. The treaty hadn't just ended a war; it had left anger behind, and later leaders used that anger to smash the limits.

On Friday, Theo's hands were sweating, but he had a plan. "I'm going to delegate the first thirty seconds to Priya," he announced, "because she helped me test my idea." Priya rolled her eyes but stood up.

"He thought Germany just bounced back after losing," she said. "So we checked the treaty. It limited the German army to 100,000 soldiers and banned Germany from having an air force."

"That's the cage," Theo went on, feeling steadier now. "A country squeezed that hard doesn't stay quiet forever. People get humiliated, and someone promises to fix it, and twenty years later you have a second war. The treaty didn't cause it alone, but it lit the fuse."

Mr. Okafor nodded slowly. "So do we have a consensus, class? Did Theo solve the why?"

Half the room said yes. Marcus in the back said, "The cage thing was cool, but the fuse thing mixed the metaphors."

"Metaphors can mix if they're on the same team," said Theo, and even Mr. Okafor laughed at that.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
story:
Claire spread the photocopy of the periodic table across the workbench, weighting the corners with a socket wrench, a coffee can of screws, and her dad's old garage-sale trophy. Somewhere in this grid of letters and numbers was the answer to the question that had been bothering her since the field trip on Tuesday. The guide at the museum had held up a case and said the bones were dated with carbon-14, and Marcus from her class had asked, "Wait, if it's fourteen, why is it still carbon?" The guide had smiled and said something about isotopes that Claire hadn't caught, because Marcus was already asking his next question. She was tired of not catching things.

Her little brother Danny crouched by the bike he was supposed to be fixing, turning the pedal with his hand instead of using tools. "You're going to void the warranty doing that," Claire said. Danny shrugged. "It's from a garage sale. There is no warranty." He watched her draw on the paper with a pencil. "What are you doing?" "Figuring something out. Carbon-14. Whether it's still carbon." "That sounds like a trick question." "That's what I thought too."

She found carbon in the sixth box down, the C with the 6 above it. She copied it onto the margin. If that 6 meant what she thought it meant, six protons, then carbon was carbon because of six, and the fourteen had to be something else. She flipped the pencil over and erased, then wrote it again. Danny leaned over her shoulder. "So is it carbon or not?" "I think it always is. I think the number of protons is the one thing that can't change." She tapped the 6. "Like, the neutrons can vary. Different versions of the same element." "Versions," Danny repeated. She remembered the guide's word surfacing. "Isotopes," she said. "They're called isotopes." Danny rolled the word around. "So carbon-14 is one of those." "Maybe. It has the same six protons, just a different count of neutrons."

She wanted to test it before she believed it. Her dad's old science book was on the shelf behind the paint cans, and she hauled it down and thumbed to the index. Under isotopes she found a table, and there it was: carbon-12, carbon-13, carbon-14, all carbon, all listed with the same proton count of 6. She read the line twice. "Ha," she said out loud.

"You were right?" Danny asked. "I was right." She felt like she'd found a hidden door in a wall she'd walked past a hundred times. Marcus had said the guide's answer was probably too complicated for them, and that had seemed plausible at the time. Now she wanted to walk up to him on Monday and say the answer in one sentence, and watch his face.

Danny went back to his bike. "Compromise," Claire said, holding up the science book. "I'll help you with that chain if you let me use the light on your workbench for my homework." Danny considered it, then slid the bike toward her. "Deal," he said. She clicked the light on over the periodic table and picked up her pencil.

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
story:
Marcus's basement smelled like lizard and microwave popcorn, which was fair, because his gecko tank took up half the room and he'd demolished a whole bag before Tyler even sat down. "It has to be done tonight," Marcus said, tapping his laptop. "The Herp Club votes on the best gecko page tomorrow, and Priya's going to win again. She's super influential. Everyone copies what she likes." So Tyler had agreed to build it, because he'd been watching coding videos all month and this was his chance to actually make something.

He opened a file called index.html and typed the heading: MARCUS'S GECKO ZONE. Then he made a second file, style.css, and wrote the rule to centre it, checking every semicolon twice. When he refreshed the page, the heading sat stubbornly against the left edge, plain black, like it hadn't heard a word he said.

"Maybe you spelled center wrong," Marcus offered.

"I didn't." Tyler read the rule out loud anyway, then changed center to CENTER, which did nothing, then changed it back. The words in style.css were fine. That was the part that bothered him. If the code was right, then something had to be happening between the two files, something he couldn't see. The page and the stylesheet were like two people in separate rooms. He stared at index.html, scrolling slowly, and noticed how short it was. Head, title, body. Nothing connecting it to anything else. Styles in a separate file had to reach the page somehow, and he couldn't find a single thread between them.

"Give up?" Marcus said. "Priya's probably got hers done already."

"One minute." Tyler searched "how does a page use a stylesheet" and read the first result, mouthing the words. Then he sat back. "It's a link tag," he said. "It goes inside the head section, and it has rel="stylesheet" in it." He typed it in, saved, and refreshed.

The heading swung to the middle of the screen and turned a deep gecko green.

Marcus leaned over his shoulder. "Add more stuff. Say geckos are carnivores. Underline it. Big." Tyler added the line, centred, italic, gleaming, and Marcus pumped his fist. Then his phone buzzed and he grabbed it, and his whole face fell. "Group chat. Priya just posted her page." He turned the screen around. Her heading was green. It was centred. It said THE GECKO ZONE.

"She stole your design?" Tyler asked.

Marcus slumped. "No. Look at the top of her page. She forgot something." Tyler peered at the screenshot, at the plain left-corner text, and started to laugh. "Her stylesheet isn't linked."

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
story:
Sadie stood at her station with three recipes spread in front of her like a puzzle with no edges. Rice, curry, flatbread, all due on the table at 3:15, and Mrs. Okoye had said she wouldn't help with timing. "That part is yours to figure out," she'd announced on day one, and she meant it.

Across from her, Marcus was already kneading his dough with dramatic flair, because he wanted the class to vote his flatbread the best in the room. He'd said so twice this period. "Watch," he told Sadie. "Mine's going to be so soft people will accuse the store bread of being cardboard."

Sadie measured two cups of water into her pot, the exact amount her recipe called for, and set it to boil. While she stirred curry paste into the pan, she did the math in her head. The flatbread needed ten minutes per side, the curry needed twenty minutes to simmer, and the rice, if she started it now, would take eighteen. She dropped the rice into the water, clapped on the lid, and turned the flame to low. That was when Marcus leaned over and pointed at her pot.

"It's going to be soupy," he warned her. "You'll have to strain it like pasta. My mom does it all the time."

Sadie hesitated, because pasta was the only thing she cooked at home, and pasta got drained, always. She reached for the colander anyway. Then she stopped and reread her recipe card. It called this the absorption method, and the water amount was measured, not random like a big pasta pot. She lifted the lid, peeked, and thought she understood: in the absorption method, rice cooks in a measured amount of water that it soaks up completely, so nothing needs draining. "No colander," she said out loud, mostly to herself. "It drinks it all." Marcus squinted at her pot like she was making this up to sabotage his win.

At 3:10 she lifted the lid again. Steam curled up, and the grains stood in neat little wells with no water left anywhere. The curry was bubbling thick, and her last flatbread puffed on the griddle. Marcus, who had timed nothing and finished his bread fifteen minutes early, now watched it cool on a plate while his curry boiled alone. "It's still probable they'll vote for me," he muttered, pouring himself some peach nectar to drink while he waited. Sadie carried all three dishes to the table at 3:14, one minute early, and set them down side by side, still steaming. Mrs. Okoye looked at the clock, then at Sadie's pot, and raised an eyebrow. "Nice," she said, and went back to grading.

Marcus leaned across the table. "Fine. Show me your rice trick on Thursday."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
story:
Nolan followed his older brother Theo through the cereal aisle, dragging his sneakers on the tile. Theo had promised to buy him a snack if Nolan helped carry bags, which was how Nolan ended up holding a list that said, in Theo's handwriting, "MILK. EGGS. DO NOT BUY MORE CEREAL. I MEAN IT."

"Can we negotiate the snack?" Nolan asked. "Two snacks. One for carrying, one for putting up with the list."

"One snack, and I pick the checkout line with the shortest queue, which is a gift in itself."

At the customer service desk, a poster caught Nolan's eye: a bike, red, with a tag that read five hundred dollars. It was the same kind of bike Theo had wanted at fifteen. "Didn't you save up for one of those?" Nolan asked.

"Yeah. Five years of birthday money and yard-work money. Three hundred bucks, sitting in the bank the whole time."

"Three hundred wasn't enough back then either?"

"It was! That's the weird part. It was exactly enough. Then." Theo frowned at the poster like it had personally insulted him.

Nolan did the math in his head, walking in a slow circle around the display bike. "The bank paid you interest every year, right? So you ended up with more than three hundred?"

"Three hundred thirty-something. They compounded it, whatever that means. My friend Ruben gets simple interest on his account, same rate, and he ended up with less than me. Compounding means the interest earns interest too, I think. Ruben was furious."

"So you had more money than five years ago," Nolan said slowly, "and the bike costs more now. Like, way more." He picked up the display bike's price tag and held it next to Theo's face, which was doing something complicated. "You gained thirty dollars and the bike gained two hundred. The bike won."

"The bike cheated."

"Did the prices rise faster than your interest rate? Is that a thing that can happen?" Nolan spun the bike's front wheel and watched it blur. "Because your balance grew, but the money buys less than it would have."

Theo groaned. "Don't say that out loud. That's like finding out the tooth fairy has a spending limit."

"It's credible, though. It's right there on the poster." Nolan pointed the price tag at it like a tiny lawyer presenting evidence. "Your account grew for five years and it doesn't cover the bike anymore. Money can be a plague that way."

"You used 'plague' wrong. Kind of. I'm too sad to argue."

Nolan put down the tag and thought hard. "Test it. Take your three thirty and a calculator, and see how much bike it buys today versus how much bike three hundred bought five years ago. Not dollars. Bikes."

Theo pulled out his phone and started typing, leaning against the cereal shelf despite his own list. "Three thirty today buys about two thirds of a bike. Three hundred back then bought a whole one." He stared at the screen. "So even with compounding, I lost bike."

"You lost bike," Nolan agreed solemnly. "That's the saddest unit I know."

Theo snapped the phone shut and grabbed the handlebars of the display model. "Fine. New plan. I negotiate a raise on my yard jobs, you carry all the bags forever, and next summer, we ride out of here together."

"Both of us on one bike?"

"We'll negotiate that too."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
story:
Leo crouched at the edge of the pond with a plastic collection jar in one hand and a folded worksheet in his back pocket. His science class had spread out along the bank, and each pair was supposed to gather pond water and then prepare an onion slide back at the picnic tables. Leo's partner, Mina, was already peeling the papery outer layer off their onion, her fingers smelling sharp enough to make his eyes sting from a foot away.

The problem was simple and enormous. Leo wanted to see cells, real ones, and label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus before the bell. If he managed it, his teacher had promised, his worksheet would go up on the classroom wall. At the tables, Mina used tweezers to pull a sliver of skin thinner than a bubble off the onion's inner layer. She laid it on the slide, added a drop of pond water, and lowered the cover slip with the careful pressure they had practiced. Leo leaned into the microscope and squinted.

Nothing. Well, almost nothing. The field was pale and blank, like looking through fogged glass. He turned the focus knob slowly, then more vigorously, but the slide stayed an empty wash of light. "Maybe we tore the skin," he said, sitting back. Mina took a look and shook her head. "It's there. I saw the edges. It's just invisible."

Leo thought about that. Invisible, not absent. He remembered that pond water full of tiny swimming things under the same lens, brownish and clear to see, and he wondered whether the difference was colour rather than size. The cells might be nearly colourless, which would explain why nothing showed up. He needed to test the idea. He looked down the supply kit on the bench: tweezers, slides, a small brown dropper bottle labeled iodine. "Stain," Mina said, reading over his shoulder. "My cousin used it last year." A drop of iodine to accompany the clear cells might be exactly the trick.

They made a fresh slide, and this time Mina placed the drop of iodine along the edge of the cover slip so it soaked underneath. Leo pressed his eye to the lens and turned the knob. The field filled with boxes, hundreds of them, walls standing out in crisp brown lines like a brick wall. "Whoa," he breathed. "Cell walls. Look." Mina pushed in beside him. There, inside each neat box, sat a darker round dot. Leo found it in cell after cell, always one, always near the middle. "Nucleus," he said, and wrote it down, then traced the thin boundary of each box and labeled the membrane too. The consequence of that one brown drop was a whole world snapping into view.

His worksheet went up on the wall that Friday, next to Mina's. Leo walked past it on his way to lunch and stopped, just for a second, to look at the little boxes again. "Still there," said Mina behind him, grinning. "Even when you can't see them."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
story:
Taylor had one motivation for signing up to cook at the farmers' market booth: she wanted to prove she could feed herself before her dad shipped out in October. The volunteer apron came with a crate of onions, a cutting board, and a chef named Rosa who spoke mostly in single words.

"Claw," Rosa said, curling her fingers under so the knuckles guided the blade. Taylor copied her, fingertips tucked away, and cut through her first onion in slow, careful slices. Her eyes watered so hard that an old man sampling salsa offered her a napkin. By the third onion her cuts were even, and she began to perspire over the portable burner where a pan of oil waited.

"Garlic and onion go in," Rosa said. "Stir." Taylor dumped both in together at the high heat and stirred, feeling like a real cook, until the onions went soft and glassy. She added the canned tomatoes, let the sauce bubble, then tasted it. Her face folded. The sauce had a burnt, bitter edge underneath the tomato, distinct and unmistakable, like someone had ground pencil shavings into it.

The old salsa man tasted it too and shook his head politely. Taylor stood over the pot and thought. The onions were soft and golden, not burnt, so the onions weren't the problem. The garlic was in tiny pieces, much smaller than the onion, and it had sat in the same hot pan the whole time. Small pieces plus long heat equaled black bits, and black bits equaled bitter. She had her theory, but she needed proof.

She fished a forkful of the dark garlic slivers out of the pot bottom and tasted them alone. Bitter. Then she minced fresh garlic and dropped it into a dry saucer for the next batch. When the new onions softened, she slid the garlic in last, gave it thirty seconds of stirring, then poured in the tomatoes. The second sauce tasted clean and sweet, and Rosa nodded once, which Taylor had already learned was a standing ovation.

"You figured out the garlic yourself," Rosa said, ladling it into sample cups. "Most people burn it twice."

Taylor handed the old salsa man a cup. He sipped, considered, and held it out for a refill. "You know," he said, "this is better than the salsa I came here to buy, and I own that booth."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
story:
Hannah stared at the blank page in her notebook and wrote "Thesis:" followed by nothing. Mr. Delgado had told the class on Monday that anyone who turned in a persuasive essay without an outline first would get the draft back ungraded, and the outline was due tomorrow at the start of English. She wanted to argue that the school should fix the dripping fountain outside the gym, but every time she tried to start, her sentences tangled into a pile of reasons with no order at all.

At lunch she sat with Priya near the vending machines and spread out her notes. "I have nine reasons," Hannah said, jabbing her pencil at the list. "Wasted water, slippery floor, kids getting detention for being late, the noise during band practice, and a bunch more. But Mr. Delgado wants three points. Three. How do I pick?"

"Pick the strongest ones," Priya said through a bite of sandwich. "Then put the rest under them, like branches."

Dylan had forty minutes before the county fair opened, and his math worksheet had other plans for him. He sat at Grandpa's kitchen table with three problems left, all of them full of letters pretending to be numbers. The first one read x + 7 = 12, and Dylan glared at it like it had insulted him.

The fair closes at nine, not at nine-ish, so do not classify your homework as optional. P.S. There's an x in the shed. It's on the workbench. That last line had to be a joke, but the shed wasn't, so Dylan marched out there anyway.

The shed smelled like oil and sawdust. On the workbench sat an old balance scale, brass pans hanging from a beam, with a tin of weights beside it. That was Grandpa's x, Dylan realized. Not the letter. The thing the letter stood for. He found a small unmarked weight in the tin, dropped it in the left pan, then added a seven-gram weight, and put a twelve-gram weight in the right pan. The beam leveled. The unknown weight plus seven made twelve. He slid the seven off the left pan and the left side rose, light and wrong, an indifferent little swing of brass. So he took a seven-gram weight off the right side too, and the beam went level again. The hidden weight was five. Subtraction undoes addition, he said out loud to the empty shed, and it sounded like something worth remembering.

He went back for the next problem, 3x = 15, carrying the scale under one arm because he didn't trust it out of his sight. In the kitchen he piled three of the unknown weights in the left pan and fifteen grams in the right. Level. Then, one by one, he removed a third of each side, taking one unknown off the left and five grams off the right, three times over, until one unknown faced five grams across a level beam. Division undoes multiplication, he said, writing x = 5. His pencil moved fast now, and the last problem fell apart in under a minute.

Dylan found a pencil stub and scrawled on the back of Grandpa's note: Found your x. It was hiding in a pan. Solved it twice. You owe me a corn dog. He pinned it to the icebox with a pineapple magnet, grabbed his jacket, and heard the truck rattle up the drive just as he reached the door. Grandpa climbed out with the fence posts and read the note over Dylan's shoulder.

Corn dog's on me, Grandpa said. But you load the truck.

Dylan already had a post in his hands.

The note was taped to Jeremy's locker before practice, folded once, in his friend Dex's blocky handwriting. "Coach gave me the go ahead to authorize you calling plays at Friday's scrimmage. "I read it." Jeremy spun a ball on his finger and let it wobble out. "I don't actually know any plays."

"You know the pick and roll."

"Sort of."

"Sort of," Dex repeated, and passed the ball hard at Jeremy's chest.

They ran it the first time and it fell apart. Jeremy dribbled left off Dex's screen, and Dex just stood there at the elbow like a fence post, watching. The defender slid around the screen, caught up, and Jeremy had to jack up a shot with a hand in his face. It clanked off the back rim.

"Move somewhere," Jeremy said, chasing the ball.

"I set the pick. That's the play."

"That can be the whole play."

Coach Ruiz blew the whistle and called them over, but only to tell them the scrimmage had been moved up, to Thursday, because the gym was scheduled for plumbing repairs on Friday. Then he walked off to argue with the maintenance man by the water fountain. Jeremy and Dex looked at each other. One day. One practice to get it right.

They ran it again, and again it broke the same way, and Jeremy started thinking instead of just getting mad. The screen worked. Dex's man got bumped every time, and Jeremy's man had to fight around. So the trouble wasn't the pick. The trouble was after. Dex froze and the whole play froze with him, and Jeremy had nowhere to throw.

"Try rolling," Jeremy said. He didn't know why that word came out, but it did. "After the pick, you turn and go to the basket. Get ready for the pass."

Dex wiped sweat off his forehead with his shirt. "So I set the screen and then I roll."

"That's why they call it a pick and roll."

They set up. Jeremy called it, jabbed left, and Dex planted himself solid. The defenders collided with the screen, and this time Dex spun, shoulders turning toward the hoop, cutting hard with his hands up. The lane opened like a door. Jeremy fired a bounce pass that hit Dex in stride, and Dex laid it in off the glass, no rim, nothing but net.

Coach Ruiz turned around from the water fountain. "Run that one Thursday," he called across the gym. "First play."

"First play," Jeremy said, and slapped the ball hard against the floor.

She moved the slide slowly left, and the dots moved with the cells, locked in place, one per box. Then she counted ten cells in a row across the field of view. Ten cells, ten darker spots, each small and round, each sitting in its own patch of cytoplasm. Dirt didn't arrange itself so politely.

"One per cell," she said out loud. "Every single one has the dot. It's not dirt, it's the nucleus."

"Then label it before you forget which one," Priya said.

Annabelle penciled in her three labels, then inked them when she was sure. "I labeled all three structures," she said, when the teacher called on her. "The nucleus is the darker round spot in each cell."

Marcus slid off his stool at station four and muttered, "Show-off."

Annabelle bent to the eyepiece one last time and traced the little row of dark dots with her finger on the glass, one, two, three, all the way to ten.

Hayden had one hour before the small demonstration contest at the science museum, and the prize was a summer spot as a junior explainer, an exceptional opportunity for a kid who had wanted to work there since third grade. The catch was the topic he had drawn from the jar: explain why Earth has seasons. He knew it had something to do with the tilt of the axis, but he could not have said it out loud to save his life.

In the astronomy room stood the giant model he loved, a lamp for the sun and a globe on a rod that could be tilted or straightened. His friend Priya from science class was there too, filling out a worksheet, and she raised an eyebrow at him pacing in front of it. "You're supposed to explain it, not glare at it," she said. "Want an alliance? You quiz me on moon phases, I'll listen to your seasons thing twice." He agreed, mostly because he needed a listener.

He started with what he remembered, spinning the globe slowly around the lamp. "So Earth goes around the sun, and it's tilted, and that makes the seasons." Priya frowned. "Tilted how? Show me." He tried to show her and realized he couldn't; the words fell apart in his hands. Frustrated, he grabbed the rod and cranked the globe upright, perfectly straight, thinking a clean model might at least look better. "Start simple," he muttered. "No tilt."

Then he stopped. With the globe straight up, he walked it all the way around the lamp, watching the light. At every point in the circle, the sunlight struck his hometown at exactly the same slant. Summer position, same angle. Winter position, same angle. Nothing changed anywhere, all the way around. "Priya, look. If Earth's axis had no tilt, the sunlight would hit each place at the same angle all year." She leaned in, shading the globe with her hand. "So then there would be almost no seasons at all," she said slowly. "It would just be the same everywhere, forever."

He tilted the globe back to its real lean and made the circuit again, and now the story told itself: the light climbed steeply on his town at one part of the circle and came in shallow and weak at the other side. He said it out loud twice, and the second time he didn't stumble once.

He came in second at the contest, one point behind a girl with a homemade eclipse diorama, and the judges told him the explainer spot was hers. Priya found him afterward by the globe, still turned honestly on its rod. "You should resign yourself to trying again next year," she said, and he almost smiled. "Maybe," he said, and gave the globe one slow spin, watching his town swing up into the light.

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
story:
Sophie pushed through the heavy glass doors of city hall carrying a shoebox of paper ballots and a poster she had made the night before. Her civics class was running a mock election in the real council chamber, and her job was to count the votes twice: once the normal way, where the candidate with the most votes in each district wins, and once under proportional representation, where seats go out in shares matching each party's share of the votes. If the two systems gave different answers, she got to stand at the microphone and explain why. If they gave the same answer, her whole presentation collapsed, and Marcus Tran would smirk at her for the rest of the semester.

She laid the ballots out on the long council table and began to count, scrutinizing each one for stray marks that might make it invalid. Three parties were running: Purple, Green, and Orange. When she finished the first count, the districts went six for Purple, four for Green, and one for Orange. Under the winner-takes-all system, Purple controlled eleven of eleven seats, even though Sophie could see on her tally sheet that plenty of people had voted Green and Orange. That part she had expected.

Then she did the proportional count, matching seats to vote shares, and stopped with her pencil in the air. Purple got five seats. Green got four. Orange got two. Nobody had more than half. She counted again, feeling a flicker of guilt, as if she must have made a mistake, because a parliament with no majority meant nobody could just vote things through. She checked the addition three times. It was right.

"We have a problem," she told the teacher, who was there only to keep time and refused to say anything more. Sophie stood at the microphone anyway. "Under the regular system, Purple wins everything and forms the government alone," she said. "Under proportional representation, Purple still has the most seats, but not a majority. So no single party can govern by itself."

"Then the mock parliament is dead," Marcus said from the second row. "Nothing can pass."

Sophie looked at the seat chart she had drawn, five purple chairs, four green, two orange, and an idea clicked into place. "Or the parties have to team up," she said. "Purple could join with either Green or Orange, and together they'd have a majority. Green and Orange together only have six, so it has to include Purple, but Purple can't do it alone."

Then came the twist. When the students took their assigned seats, the Purple leader announced that her party would rather sit in opposition than share power with anyone, because coalisons, she declared, looked weak. The chamber went silent. Sophie realized the rules forced negotiation, but they could not force agreement. So she proposed a vote on which partner Purple would accept, and when the Purple caucus voted, they chose Orange, the smaller party, because the Green students had run a biased campaign that mocked their platform, and Purple had not forgotten.

The Orange leader walked across the chamber and shook the Purple leader's hand, and Sophie wrote the two words on her poster in block letters: "coalition government."

Annabelle had one period left before she had to show the fundraiser totals to the whole seventh grade, and her spreadsheet was still a mess of numbers with no total and no chart. Mr. Ruiz had given the class exactly one demo yesterday, and then the server had gone down, so today she was on her own in the computer lab, typing scores from a crumpled printout of the candy sale.

She entered the numbers into column B, rows two through ten: forty-two, seventeen, thirty-three, all the way down. Then she needed the total, so she clicked on the first empty cell that looked right, B10, right beneath the last number, and typed =SUM(B2:B10). That seemed sensible. "Fix mine too," Priya said. "I did the same thing."

Annabelle moved the sum on Priya's sheet too, then highlighted her own numbers, clicked Insert, and chose a bar chart. Blue bars climbed the screen, one for each homeroom, and she could see at a glance that room 214 had crushed everyone else.

The bell rang. Annabelle saved the file twice, grabbed the printout, and headed for the door with her laptop under her arm.

"Show them the bars," Priya called after her. "Start with the tallest one."

story:
Gavin had one goal for Saturday: learn to make pasta sauce from scratch so he could stop eating the cafeteria's grey, gluey version, which his friend Dario called "straight-up toxic." Dario's older sister Priya had agreed to teach them, mostly because their mother was at work and someone had to make sure they didn't burn the house down. Dario's little sister Mia sat on the counter swinging her legs; she'd had a vaccine that morning and her arm was too sore to do anything but supervise.

"First, the onion," Priya said, setting a cutting board on the counter and handing Gavin a knife. "Bend your fingers under so your knuckles guide the blade. Claw grip." Gavin curled his fingertips back like she showed him and pressed down on the onion. The knife squashed the skin and slid sideways, skating off the onion and thunking onto the board. He tried again, pushing harder, and it skated again, this time toward his thumb.

"Stop, stop." Priya took the knife and swapped it for a different one from the drawer, thinner and shinier. "Sharp knives are safer. They need less pressure, so they're less likely to slip off the food." Gavin eyed it warily, but when he drew it through the onion, it sank clean through without any pushing at all. Slice after slice fell away, and his knuckles, held steady in the claw grip, never came close to the edge. Dario, who was peeling garlic, kept leaning over to watch.

While the onion softened in the pan, Dario tried to chop a tomato with the dull knife Gavin had set aside. He bore down on it, and the blade shot off the slick skin and rocketed the tomato across the counter. Mia reached out with her good arm and caught it before it hit the floor, then set it back on the board with enormous dignity. "Your sore arm didn't hinder you there," Gavin said, and Mia shrugged like a goalie who had expected nothing less.

Priya slid the sharp knife back to Dario, and the tomato gave up without a fight. They crushed the tomatoes into the pan, and Gavin stirred while Mia directed him in a clockwise-only policy she had invented. By the time the sauce smelled like an actual kitchen instead of a cafeteria line, Gavin had chopped two onions without a single slip, and he was feeling indestructible.

Then his eyes began to sting, and he blinked, and suddenly he was crying so hard he had to leave the board. Mia hopped down, patted his back, and picked up the sharp knife to scrape the last of the onion into the pan, quick as anything. "Don't worry," she said kindly, handing him a paper towel. "It's only me who's dangerous."

story:
Abigail fed quarters into the machine like she had watched her mother do a hundred times, except this time her mother was not beside her. "Sort the darks from the lights," Mom had said on the phone that morning, "and check every pocket. Every one." Then she had laughed, which Abigail did not think was fair, and hung up to catch her flight to Denver.

The dark pile went in first: her black jeans, her brother's gray hoodie, her navy shirt printed with little bees that looked ready to pollinate a whole garden. She poured the detergent, closed the door, and watched the drum start its slow spin. Thirty-eight minutes, the display said. She sat on the orange plastic bench and remembered being eight, standing in this exact laundromat, when Mom had pulled a crumpled receipt out of Dad's jacket and held it up like evidence in a trial. "This is why we check pockets," Mom had announced to the whole room. A man folding towels two machines over had nodded solemnly, as if agreeing to a treaty. Abigail had laughed so hard she had to sit on the floor.

Now the washer thumped and sloshed, and she thought about her own cargo shorts, the khaki ones, which were in the machine right at this moment. Had she checked those pockets? She tried to remember. She had checked the hoodie. She had definitely checked the hoodie. The shorts had gone in so fast, right off the bathroom floor, and there had been something in the side pocket yesterday, a tissue maybe, or a wrapper, she could not picture it. She stood up, walked over, and stared at the round window. Soap and water and dark fabric tumbled together, and there was no way to see inside a pocket from here. She could stop the machine, but that would waste the quarters, and she only had two left. She sat back down and argued with herself for the full thirty-eight minutes.

When the load came out, she knew the answer before she spread anything flat. Every dark item was speckled with white, like snow had fallen only on her clothes. One tissue, somewhere, had broken apart in the wash and scattered shreds over everything, every single piece in the load. Her bee shirt looked like the bees were flying through a blizzard. She picked off shred after shred, and the bits stuck and clung and would not quit, and she thought about how one small forgotten thing could do all this, and about other small forgotten things, like the note she had never answered for her friend Priya last spring. She kept picking.

An hour later, mostly clean, the clothes went into the dryer. She folded the bee shirt in a neat diagonal, corner to corner, the way Mom did, and set it on top of the stack. Then she pulled out the cargo shorts, turned them upside down, and shook them hard over the trash bin. A single surviving shred of tissue floated down. "You," she told it, "almost got away with it," and she dropped the shorts back in for another rinse.

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
story:
Brooke sat cross-legged on the living room carpet with her laptop open on the coffee table, a bowl of crackers beside her and 214 rows of survey answers glowing on the screen. She had asked every student in the school one question: should the spring dance have a live band or a DJ? Her little brother's friend Jonah had voted three times, which she had deduced from the fact that nobody else in fifth grade was named "Jonoth." She deleted the fake rows and started over.

In the kitchen, her dad was wrestling with the plumbing under the sink, and every so often a wrench clanged against a pipe. "It's not you," he called out at one point. "The pipe's older than you are." Brooke barely heard him. She had built her first pivot table, dropping Grade into the rows and Band or DJ into the columns, and the counts stared back at her. Eighth grade had the biggest numbers on every single answer. Band, DJ, the "no opinion" option, everything. Eighth grade won it all.

She leaned back against the couch. It seemed obvious that eighth graders were the most opinionated kids in the school, but something about that bothered her. There were simply more of them; she remembered the crowded eighth-grade hallway from last year and the thin little line of sixth graders at lunch. Maybe the grade with the most students would win every count no matter what anyone actually thought. She couldn't see opinions directly, but she could test the idea.

She clicked through the pivot table options until she found something called "Show Values As" and chose to display each count as a percentage of its column total. The numbers shifted. Now every grade's answers added up to one hundred percent within its own column. Eighth grade's advantage vanished like a magic trick run backward. On the band-versus-DJ question, sixth grade turned out to be the most divided, with almost a perfect split, while eighth graders leaned hard toward the DJ. She had almost published a report saying the opposite of the truth.

"Ha!" she said out loud.

Her dad poked his head around the doorway, a drip falling from his elbow. "Ha, what?"

"The eighth graders only looked like they won everything because there are more of them," Brooke said. "Percentages fixed it." She turned the screen so he could see.

He grinned at her, and the grin was infectious, and he said, "That's more than I can say for this pipe." She thought about last fall, when she had guessed about the lost field day money and blamed the wrong kid, and how she'd sworn afterward to stop guessing. She hadn't exactly kept that promise today, but this time she had checked before believing herself.

Brooke copied the pivot table into her report and typed the title: "What the Whole School Really Thinks."

story:
Riley stood in the garage next to the old dryer, holding her brother's white dress shirt at arm's length like evidence. "It was in here all night," she said. Marcus snatched it and turned it toward the window light. Every crease from the drum had set into the fabric, sharp lines across the chest and sleeves.

"The interview's at ten," Marcus said. He rubbed a fold between his fingers as if he could erase it. "This is the only shirt that isn't wrinkled, or it was." He had been talking about the job at the bike shop all week, and now he stood there in his socks, staring at the shirt like it had betrayed him on purpose.

Riley thought back to Sunday, when she had started learning laundry so she could take the chore over from their mom. She had sorted the colors, learned that the whites went in hot, and folded a whole basket of towels while they were still warm from the dryer. Those towels had come out smooth. She remembered pulling the last towel out minutes after the cycle ended, soft and flat, and stacking it in a neat pile with perfect symmetry, corners matched. But the shirt had sat crumpled in the drum for twelve hours after the cycle stopped, cooling in a heap.

"I have an idea," Riley said. "The towels were fine because I took them out right away and folded them. Watch." She shoved the shirt back into the dryer, alone, and set it for twenty minutes. Marcus paced between the car and the workbench, tapping a wrench against his palm. When the timer buzzed, Riley opened the door and pulled the shirt out fast, before it could sit there and cool down crumpled again. She laid it flat on the folding table and smoothed the sleeves with both hands, then folded along the same creases the fabric already wanted. She hung it on the nail by the door and stood back.

Marcus held it up. The old lines had almost vanished, and the collar lay flat. "Okay, that's actually wearable." He buttoned it to the top and looked at himself in the garage window reflection. "If I get this job, I'm buying you a pizza."

"You're buying me a pizza anyway," Riley said. She pulled the next load from the washer, a tangle of his synthetic running shirts, and fed them into the drum. "And I'm setting a timer. Nothing stays in this dryer after the buzz."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
story:
Stella stood at the lectern in the empty church, the paper shaking slightly in her hand. "A reading from the letter of Saint Paul," she began, and then the words slid sideways, the way they had every afternoon that week. She stopped, exhaled, and stared at the stained glass window of the dove as if it might whisper the next line.

Her quinceañera was three weeks away, and she had assumed the party was the whole thing: the dress already hanging in Tía Rosa's closet, the playlist Marco was building on his phone. Then Father Ruiz had asked whether she wanted to do one of the readings at the Mass that opens the celebration, the Mass of thanksgiving for her fifteenth birthday. She had said yes before she understood what yes would cost, and now she regretted it a little, the way she still regretted quitting piano in fourth grade after one bad recital.

In the third pew, Marco looked up from his phone. "You dropped a whole verse. Also, Auntie Lupita texted. She wants to know if the reading is the same one Abuela did at hers."

"Nobody has Abuela's reading," Stella said. But Marco was already scrolling through his database of family files, the giant folder he kept of old programs and party invitations. He found a folded bulletin from 1996, and there it was, printed in small type: the reading Abuela had given, the same one Stella was struggling with now.

Stella came down from the lectern and took the bulletin. She noticed something she had missed before. When she tried to recite from memory, she kept starting at the beginning, and by the middle her mind felt crowded and vulnerable, like a shelf with too much on it. But when she whispered the lines while walking slowly down the aisle, one phrase for every two steps, the words stopped orbiting her head and settled into her feet. She tried it again, and again, and the missing verse surfaced on its own, caught between the rhythm of her steps and the smell of old incense.

"Twenty-six times she probably did it just like this," Stella said, tucking Abuela's bulletin into her pocket. She walked back up the aisle, heels clicking on the stone, and began without the paper. "A reading from the letter of Saint Paul," she said, and this time she did not stop.

"Keep going," Marco whispered from the pew.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
story:
Levi locked the bathroom door and gripped the edge of the sink. In twenty minutes he had to stand up in front of his whole class and give a speech, and his hands were shaking like the time he'd tried to carry six textbooks at once. His heart pounded so loud he could hear it in his ears. He stared at his pale face in the mirror and made himself think like a scientist. Something invisible was happening inside him, and there had to be a way to measure it, and maybe a way to change it.

He tried to remember last month, when his cousin Priya had to give a student council speech. He flashed back to sitting beside her at the kitchen table while she dragged her finger slowly around an invisible square on the tabletop, again and again, like she was tracing a picture frame nobody else could see. "What are you doing?" he had asked. "Box breathing means breathing in for a count of four, holding for four, breathing out for four and holding for four, then repeating the pattern," she had said, and kept tracing. He'd laughed at her then. He wasn't laughing now.

Levi raised his finger and drew one side of a square in the air above the sink, breathing in for four counts. He held his breath along the second side, let it out along the third, and waited through the fourth. Then he did it again. The shaking in his hands slowed like a fan winding down. He kept going, tracing the invisible box, and made a discovery: if he counted with the square instead of watching the clock, the gradual loosening in his shoulders was something he could actually feel happening. He tested it, speeding up on purpose, and his heart started hammering again. Slow square, calm. Fast square, panic. The pattern was real, like a hidden rule he'd just proven.

That was when he heard a sniffle from behind the shower curtain. Levi pulled it back and found his little sister, Nadia, sitting in the dry tub with her knees pulled up to her chin. Her spelling bee was the same afternoon as his speech, in the other fifth and sixth grade room down the hall.

"The words are so hard this year," she whispered. "I'm not even a good candidate to win. Why would they pick hard words like 'flourish' if nobody can spell them?"

Levi sat down on the edge of the tub. "Give me your hand." He turned her palm up and drew one side of a square on it with his finger, slow and steady, breathing in for four. She frowned, then copied him, holding her breath, letting it out, waiting, around and around. Her shoulders came down from around her ears.

Ten minutes later, Levi stood at the front of his classroom. He traced a small square along the edge of the podium where nobody could see, and his voice came out steady and strong. Down the hall, through the open door, he heard a judge call out, "Flourish. F-L-O-U-R-I-S-H." A pause, then applause, and a voice he knew saying, "Correct."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
story:
The courthouse smelled like old paper and floor wax, and Sebastian's class had been told to find one case happening today and take notes on it. Most kids picked the flashy one on the second floor, but Sebastian had drifted into a smaller courtroom where a man was arguing that his landlord had no right to post rules banning tenants from gathering in the lobby. The judge kept saying the word "ambiguous," pointing at a clause nobody could agree on, and Sebastian filled half his page before he realized the argument had snagged on something he didn't understand: which rights the tenants actually had in the first place.

He thought of the park. His park, or what had been his park until the fence went up around the duck pond two weeks ago. His friends wanted to march in front of City Hall on Saturday, holding signs, and Sebastian had said maybe. What he hadn't told anyone was that last spring, when his older cousin got in trouble for a heated argument at a community meeting, Sebastian had stood in the back and said nothing. He'd told himself he wasn't part of it. He was eleven then, and it was easier to be eleven and invisible. That memory sat in him like a stone whenever the park came up now.

In the corridor outside the courtroom, his classmate Priya was squinting at her phone. "My dad says we could get in trouble for the march," she said. "Like, is it even allowed?"

"That's the thing," Sebastian said. "Allowed how? By who?" He typed charter into the library kiosk near the water fountain, then charter freedoms, and the screen gave him a page with numbered sections. He scrolled past Section 1, which sounded vague, and stopped at Section 2. "Here," he said, and read aloud: "Section 2 of the Canadian Charter protects fundamental freedoms, including freedom of religion, freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association."

"Priya tapped the screen. "Peaceful assembly. That's us. Signs, marching, no shouting matches."

"And expression, so the signs count too," Sebastian said. He read it again, slower, testing it against Saturday in his head. Assembly meant being together in public. Association meant his friends could organize it as a group without that being the problem. Expression meant the cardboard signs weren't decoration. He copied the whole sentence into his notebook, then underneath he wrote: we can stand together and say what we want, as long as we're peaceful. It wasn't the fancy version. It was his version, and it fit on two lines.

"Wait," Priya said, grinning. "Does this mean your right to complain about my playlist is constitutionally protected?"

"No," Sebastian said. "Your playlist invades everyone's rights. That's different."

She laughed, and their teacher called them back toward the bus. Sebastian slid his notebook into his bag, thinking about his cousin, about standing in the back of that meeting, and about Saturday. This time he knew which section he was standing under.

"Pick you up at the pond at ten," he told Priya. "We'll make the signs Friday night. And Priya? Bring the bad markers, the ones you like."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
story:
Maya's basement smelled like old carpet and microwave popcorn, and the two of them had until six o'clock, when Maya's mom would drive Ella home. That gave them ninety minutes to finish the web page for their group project on famous court trials, and the heading still sat stubbornly on the left side of the screen.

"Try it again," Maya said, pulling her knees up onto the folding chair. Ella retyped the line in the style section, saved the file, and hit refresh. The words "The Trial of the Century" stayed glued to the left margin like a defendant refusing to leave the witness stand. Ella stared at it. The code looked right to her. She had written what she meant to write.

"Maybe the computer's broken," Maya offered. Ella shook her head. Computers didn't get moody. Something in the file had to be the hidden cause, some rule she couldn't see directly, and if she could infer what it was, she could fix it. She read the line out loud, slowly: "text-align: centre;" Then she read the paragraph tag above it, and the body tag, checking each one against the example in Maya's notebook from the library book. Everything matched except one thing. The book spelled it "center."

She looked at the word for a long moment. We spell it centre. The book spelled it the American way. Maybe the browser only understood one spelling, and hers simply didn't count. It was a guess, but it was easy to test. She deleted the "r" and the "e," swapped them, and typed "center." Save. Refresh.

The heading glided to the middle of the page and stayed there, perfectly centred, the way she had pictured it all afternoon.

"Whoa," Maya said, leaning in. "So it only works with the American spelling?"

"That's the only difference I changed," Ella said. She scrolled up and double-checked to be sure. Same tag, same punctuation, same place. One word, different letters.

Maya laughed and flopped back against the couch cushion. "I felt so gullible five minutes ago, like the page was playing a trick on me." They split the rest of the popcorn and divided the work: Maya wrote the section about the verdict, and Ella built a second page with a smaller heading at the top, typing "center" twice, carefully, both times. When Maya's mom called down the stairs at five fifty, Ella closed the laptop and slid it into her backpack, zipping it shut.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
story:
The periodic table poster had come free with a box of cereal, and Nicholas had taped it to the garage wall between the shovel and a coil of garden hose. He stood in front of it with his friend Marco, who was holding a crumpled worksheet from summer science camp.

"Question three," Marco said. "How many protons in a neon atom?"

"You just asked me carbon. Give me a second."

"That was two questions ago. Camp starts Monday. If you flunk the placement quiz, you get stuck in the beginner group with the kids who think a beaker is a cup."

Nicholas scanned the poster. The boxes ran left to right in rows, and each one held a name, a symbol, and at least two numbers. That was the problem. Which number meant what?

"Ten," he said, guessing.

"Why ten?"

He pointed at the neon box in the top row. "It says ten right there."

"There are two tens up there somewhere, I think. My brother said one of them is heavier stuff, like an approximate weight. He said it's not exact."

Nicholas looked again. The number above the symbol was a small whole number, six for carbon, two for helium, ten for neon. The number below the symbol was messier, like 20.180. That one had to be the inexact one. So the small number had to be the one that counted something.

He pulled a marker from the workbench and wrote on a scrap of sandpaper: helium 2, carbon 6, oxygen 8. "Every box has this same number," he said. "It's like an address. Hydrogen is one, and it climbs by one all the way across."

"So?"

"So the boxes are in order. Hydrogen first, helium second. The number isn't random, it's the order." He tapped the poster. "And if every atom of an element is the same, the number has to count something inside the atom. Something every one of them has."

"Could be electrons," Marco said.

"Could be. But it counts protons." Nicholas paused. "That's what the top number is. The atomic number. Atomic number ten for neon."

Marco checked the answer key folded in his back pocket. He unfolded it slowly, the way he did when he wanted the silence to hurt. "Ten protons," he read. "Neon, atomic number ten, ten protons."

Nicholas picked up the marker again. He wrote 10 next to NE on the sandpaper scrap and set it under the poster like a trophy.

"Question four," Marco said. "Sulfur."

Nicholas ran his finger along the third row, past the gap where the poster had torn, and stopped on a yellow box. He was already writing the number before he said it out loud.

"Sixteen."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
story:
Charlie found the letter taped to her locker at the rink, folded twice, her mother's handwriting slanting across the page. "Your brother ran his first eight hundred today and finished ninth. He started too fast again. Maybe you'll figure out what he never did." Charlie read it twice, then stuffed it in her jacket pocket and laced her skates, though she wasn't there to skate. She was there because Coach Preeti had arranged for the running club to use the oval path outside the rink, the one looped around the parking lot, marked in chalk every few strides. It wasn't a track, but Preeti had measured it with a wheel and announced that one full loop was equivalent to a quarter of a proper outdoor track, so eight loops would stand in for the real thing. "The eight hundred," Preeti had said on the first day, "on a standard four-hundred-metre outdoor track, is exactly two laps. Two. That's the whole race. So it's really two races: a first lap and a second lap, and the second one is where it's won or lost."

Charlie had lost count of her loops twice already that week, and today she intended to fix it. Her idea was simple: she would carry eight small washers in her left hand and transfer one to her right at every chalk mark, so the count would live in her fists where she could feel it. "You look like you're doing magic," said Dana, jogging up beside her, breath steaming in the cold air off the rink.

"I'm regulating my brain," Charlie said, and showed her the washers. "It lies to me when I'm tired. This doesn't."

They started together. The first loop felt easy, almost lazy, and Charlie had to hold herself back the way Preeti had drilled, keeping her legs loose, saving the economy of her stride for later. At each mark she moved a washer, feeling the small cold weight shift from palm to palm. Dana pulled ahead on the fifth loop, and Charlie's legs began to burn. On the sixth loop her mind made its move. It whispered that this was the last one, that the finish was around the next bend, and her body believed it before her hands did. She surged, arms driving, passed Dana, sprinted for the rink wall with everything left in her.

Then she opened her fists. Two washers in the right hand. Six in the left. Six loops done, two to go, and she was only half finished. Her legs turned to water, Dana swept past her, and Charlie crossed the line twenty seconds behind, gasping against the boards while the Zamboni rattled past behind the glass.

Afterward she sat on the bench inside, skaters carving circles beyond the glass, and wrote back to her mother on the back of the letter. "I kicked a lap too early because I forgot the race is two laps on a four-hundred track, exactly two, and I was only in the second one. Now I count it in my hands. I lost today but I know exactly why." She read it over, then added one more line and signed it. Outside, Dana was waiting by the doors with two waters and a grin, holding one out.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
story:
Eleanor slapped the photocopied pages of the settler's diary onto the library table so hard that Marcus, sitting perpendicular to her in the next chair, nearly dropped his granola bar. "This diary is my primary source," she said, jabbing the page. "Mr. Alvarez says a primary source is like a window into the past. This guy, Amos Blankenship, crossed the trail in 1852 and wrote about it every single night. This is going to be the best essay in the class."

Marcus leaned over and squinted. "He writes about his oxen like they're his best friends. Look, he named one President." They both giggled. "President the ox. That's actually amazing." Eleanor read aloud a line about grass "stretching empty to the horizon, free for the taking," and Marcus stopped chewing. "Free for the taking," he repeated. "Didn't other people already live out there? Like, entire nations?"

Eleanor flipped through the pages, hunting. Amos wrote about river crossings and sore feet and President's mood swings, but nowhere did she find anything about how the Native American nations whose lands the trail crossed saw the same events. She checked the last page, then the first, feeling like she'd dropped her ice cream cone on the sidewalk. "A primary source shows one person's view," she said slowly. "Amos's view. Nobody else's."

"That's a problem for your essay," Marcus said cheerfully, because it wasn't his essay. Eleanor stuck her tongue out at him. Then she had an idea, and she tested it the way you test whether a pudding cup is actually sealed: with a push. If Amos couldn't tell the other side, maybe a different primary source could. She marched to the computer, typed in the names of the nations along the trail route, and started hunting for interviews, oral histories, anything recorded from their side.

Twenty minutes later she was scribbling notes so fast her pen squeaked. She found an oral history, passed down and later written down, describing the same rivers Amos had forded, and it didn't just disagree with his diary, it flat-out contradicted it. Amos wrote "empty land"; the oral history described busy trade routes, villages, and wagon ruts cutting straight through planting grounds. Same events, two windows, facing different directions.

Mr. Alvarez stopped at their table on his way past. "Finding everything you need, Eleanor?"

"Better than that," she said. "I found two windows." She held up her notes and Amos's diary side by side. "Guess which ox doesn't show up in the second one."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
story:
Camille stood in the wings of the community theatre, listening to the wooden floor creak under the feet of the advanced improv troupe. She had one week to learn what they made look easy. The spring showcase was open to everyone, and her partner, Theo, had already signed them up.

Their first practice went badly. Theo walked onto the empty stage, mimed pulling a heavy rope, and said, "Careful, this anchor is slipping." Camille froze. "There's no rope," she said. "We're just standing on a stage." The room went quiet, and Theo's arms dropped to his sides. Someone in the front row actually laughed, but not in a good way.

Ms. Rojas, the troupe's oldest member and unofficial mentor, gave Camille a ride home that night. She didn't lecture. She only said, "What you did back there has a name. Blocking." Then she turned up the radio and let Camille think.

Camille remembered the troupe's last showcase, weeks before she'd joined. Two boys had done a scene where one said, "Your dog is chewing my shoe," and the other answered, "No, that's not my dog." The audience had gone quiet right there, and the scene had stumbled to a stop, like a car rolling into a ditch. At the time Camille thought the second boy had just been unfunny. Now she wondered if there was a rule underneath it. Rejecting your partner's offer, or even ignoring it, seemed to stop the scene from moving forward. And maybe the opposite was true too. If she accepted every offer and added something of her own, the scene might build instead of die.

The next practice, she decided to test it. Theo started a scene by sitting on an invisible chair and announcing, "Grandma, the spaceship landed in our cabbage patch." Instead of denying him, Camille hobbled over as a grandmother, squinting at the window. "Then get my vacuum cleaner, sweetheart. I've always wanted to fight aliens with it." Theo's whole face changed. He grabbed the imaginary vacuum, and suddenly they were blasting cabbage thieves into orbit while the new kids in the audience laughed for real.

They ran it again, and again, and Camille noticed something. Every time Theo offered something, no matter how strange, and she said yes and added more, the scene grew richer. Every time either of them hesitated, it went flat, an impoverished little skit about nothing. "You changed your mind about me," Theo said at the end of practice, still holding the invisible vacuum. "Last week you looked at me like I was crazy."

"I thought you were breaking the rules," Camille admitted. "Turns out you were making them."

At the showcase, Theo turned to her on stage, held out an empty hand, and said, "Ready? The anchor's slipping." Camille gripped the rope.
