activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
story:
Jace pressed his pencil so hard against the paper that the vanishing point turned into a small gray bruise. All his lines were supposed to meet there, and most of them did, but the street on his page still looked like it was falling sideways into a ditch. Mr. Okonkwo had said only one thing all period: "One point. Everything runs to it." That was it. No rescue mission, no demonstration on Jace's paper. Art class had quietly become Jace's most difficult subject, which was annoying, because he had signed up for it thinking it would be an easy A.

"Switch seats with me," said Priya, sliding her drawing across the table. Her street looked like a real street. Buildings on both sides, curb, sidewalk seams, all of it rushing toward a tidy dot.

"Why? Yours works."

"Because I want to draw the window side, and you've got the window seat." She pointed across the room, where their friend Dario was already set up at the tall table by the glass, looking down at the parking lot. "He's doing the street from up there. I'm doing it from down here. Same street, different height."

Jace looked at her drawing, then at his own, and felt the familiar itch of a mystery. Her horizon, the line where the vanishing point sat, was low on the page, barely above the car roofs she'd sketched in. His own horizon sat near the top. He had put it there because the top of the page seemed like a reasonable spot for a line, which, he now suspected, was a completely arbitrary decision.

Last semester flashed back to him, sharp and embarrassing. He'd argued with Dario for a full ten minutes about whether their comic panels were the same size, holding a ruler like a sword, only to discover he'd been measuring from the wrong edge the whole time. Dario had never let it go. "Measure twice, Jace," he said every time they split a pizza. Jace had made an adversary out of a ruler that day, and the ruler had won. He wasn't going to do that again with a horizon line.

He carried his paper to the window and crouched down, then stood on his toes, then crouched again, watching where the far end of the parking lot seemed to touch the sky. Down low, everything towered over him; up high, he was looking down on the hoods of cars. Back at his seat, he erased his high horizon and redrew it low, near the bottom, then recalibrated every line so they ran toward the relocated dot. He slowed down, checking each one against the edge of the ruler twice before committing.

The street changed under his pencil. The buildings rose like cliffs. The doors loomed. It looked less like a map now and more like standing at the bottom of the block on a summer afternoon, when he was eight and the ice cream truck's music came around the corner and everything seemed taller than him. Whether he'd liked being small like that, or had just gotten used to it, he honestly couldn't decide, and the drawing wasn't going to answer for him.

"Whoa," said Priya, leaning over. "Yours looks like a kid drew it."

"Thanks," Jace said, and then, hearing it, "I mean, thanks."

"Come here," Dario called from the window, waving his paper. His horizon sat high on the page, and his street lay below it like something spread out on a table, roofs visible, cars small and distant. He held it up against the glass, comparing. "Same street," he said slowly, "totally different view. That's wild."

"That's the whole point," Priya said. "Yours looks like the window drew it."

Jace set his drawing beside Dario's on the sill and stepped back to look at both. "Mine's from the curb," he said. "Kid height. Yours is from upstairs." He tapped the low horizon, then the high one. "I want to try one in the middle next."

Dario grinned and slid his ruler across the sill. "Measure twice," he said.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
story:
Harrison had exactly one free period before the code club demo, and he was spending it in the computer lab staring at a program that refused to behave. His prime checker worked for 7, it worked for 13, it even worked for 100, which was satisfyingly not prime. But the moment he typed 0, the screen announced that 0 was prime, which felt like being told his shoe was a bird.

"Try negative five," said Priya from the next computer, leaning over with the confidence of someone who had already broken her own program six times. "If it says that's prime too, I'm going to laugh."

He typed it. IS PRIME, said the screen.

"That's not even a little bit prime," Priya said. "My little brother knows that, and he thinks cartilage is a type of cheese."

Harrison scrolled through his code. The loop started at 2 and checked every possible divisor up to the number. For 0, it never found anything to reject it with, so the program fell through to the "prime" message. Same for 1. Same for every negative number he could throw at it. The loop started at 2, and there was simply nothing below that doing any work. He dragged his fingers through his hair. "So the loop can't catch them. They just slip past."

"Then catch them before the loop," Priya said, as if it were obvious, and stole his chair's spare cushion.

He typed a check at the top of the program: if the number was below 2, print NOT PRIME, then stop right there and never even start the divisor loop. It felt almost too simple. He saved the file twice, because his flash drive was old but durable, having survived a full year at the bottom of his backpack next to a leaking water bottle and a bag of gravel, or what had once been pretzels.

He typed 0. NOT PRIME. He typed 1. NOT PRIME. He typed negative 5, negative 12, and, feeling reckless, negative 900. NOT PRIME, every time, in neat gray letters.

"Okay, that's actually kind of beautiful," Priya admitted.

At the demo that afternoon, Mr. Alvarez asked for a volunteer number, and Marcus, who had once told Harrison that programming was for people who hated sunlight, called out "zero" with a grin. Harrison typed it in. NOT PRIME. Marcus's grin folded in on itself like a compromised sandwich.

"Fine," Marcus said. "Do negative four million."

Harrison's fingers were already moving.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
story:
Arthur had exactly forty minutes to finish the museum's element scavenger hunt, and the final clue was the worst one: "Find the simplest element on the periodic table, then document its name and atomic number." The prize was a glow-in-the-dark keychain shaped like a dinosaur, and Arthur wanted it the way a cat wants an open tuna can.

He planted himself in front of the giant periodic table painted on the wall of the chemistry hall. It looked like a plate of colored squares, some squat, some tall, one section floating below like an afterthought. His best friend Nadia leaned against the railing, eating pretzels with the calm of someone who had already finished.

"Simplest," Arthur muttered. "Simplest how? Shortest name? Tin. Three letters. Done." He started to write it down.

"Bold strategy," Nadia said, peering over his shoulder. "Also, tin is in the floating part, so good luck feeling proud about that."

Arthur stopped, pencil hovering. The clue sheet had a second line he'd skipped: "Hint: what does the atomic number count?" He looked back at the wall. Every square had a name, a symbol, and a small whole number in the corner. Gold had 79. Carbon had 6. The numbers went up as he moved right and down, like a ramp, then hit a plateau in the middle where they just climbed steadily, square after square, all the way to 112.

"If the numbers go up like that," he said slowly, "then the simplest one should have the smallest number. Which means the top." His eyes climbed the columns. The top of the very first column, in the top left corner, was a single square with a 1 on it. Hydrogen.

"So hydrogen is number one," Nadia said, chewing. "Ironic, since you nearly picked tin off the bottom."

"The atomic number counts protons," Arthur read off the sign below the wall. He tapped the hydrogen square. "So one means one proton. Every hydrogen atom has exactly one proton." He said it again, quieter, testing it like a loose tooth. "That's why it's the simplest. Nothing has a smaller number, so nothing has fewer."

Nadia pointed at the helium square next to it, with its little 2. "So that one's got two."

"Two protons, yeah." Arthur grinned and flipped to a blank page in his notebook. He wrote H, then drew one dot for the proton, then a lopsided atom with a single dot in the middle like a lonely period at the end of a sentence. He added a hat on the atom, because it deserved something for being first.

At the desk, the docent checked his answer, stamped his sheet, and dropped the dinosaur keychain into his palm. Arthur held it up to the hydrogen square on the wall.

"Sorry, hydrogen. You'll always be number one to me, but the dino glows."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
story:
Muhammad's social studies teacher had given every seventh grader the same assignment: go somewhere public, find one right listed in the country's constitution, and explain it in your own words to a real person. That was why Muhammad was standing outside the gymnasium of Lincoln Elementary on a Tuesday morning in November, holding his notebook like a shield.

The gym had been turned into a polling station. Folding tables stretched in rows, and machines at the far wall emitted a soft, steady beep whenever someone finished voting. A long line of adults snaked past the drinking fountains, everybody stamping their feet against the cold that leaked in whenever the doors opened. Muhammad's plan was simple. He would ask a poll worker to let him read the copy of the Constitution the library kept on display, pick a right, and explain it to his grandfather, who was somewhere in that line.

He found the display case first, right beside the "Vote Here" sign. The pages behind the glass were open to the amendments. He read down the list, mouthing the words, until one line made him stop. The Fifth Amendment. He knew that phrase. His older cousin watched a police show every Sunday, and the suspects on it were always saying, "I plead the Fifth," right before the dramatic music played. Muhammad had never known what it actually meant.

He copied the line into his notebook, letter by letter. Then he walked back toward the line to find his grandfather, and that was when he saw the problem. A man at the second table was arguing with a poll worker, his voice rising. "You can't make me tell you who I voted for," the man was saying. "I don't have to answer that."

Muhammad slowed down. He stood near the drinking fountain, pretending to fill his water bottle, though it was already full. The poll worker, a woman with silver braids, kept her voice low. "Sir, nobody's asking who you voted for. We only need your name for the check-in list." The man frowned, repeated his refusal, and the woman wrote something on a slip of paper and handed it to him. He took it and moved along, still grumbling.

Muhammad's heart was beating fast, though he couldn't have said why. Something clicked. He looked at the line in his notebook: no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves. The man at the table had borrowed the idea, maybe from a TV show, and Muhammad suddenly understood both what the man had meant and what he had gotten wrong. It was about criminal cases. Being a witness against yourself.

His grandfather was third from the front now, so Muhammad had maybe two minutes. He practiced under his breath, crossing out his first attempt, which sounded like he'd swallowed a textbook. His second try was plainer.

"Abu," he said when his grandfather reached the table, "I figured out my assignment." He held up the notebook. "The Fifth Amendment says no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves. Like, if someone got arrested, they don't have to answer questions that would get them in trouble."

His grandfather read the notebook page, then looked at him for a long moment. "That's an eloquent way to put it," he said. "Now tell me why that fellow at the table was wrong."

Muhammad glanced back toward the second table, where the silver-braided worker was already helping the next voter. The man with the slip of paper stood by the machines, hesitating, the paper crumpled slightly in his fist.

"I think," Muhammad said slowly, "he thought it meant he never had to answer anything. But it's only criminal cases."

His grandfather nodded toward the voting machines. "Go ask her," he said. "The worker. Ask what the paper says."

Muhammad looked at the paper in the man's hand, then at the worker's calm face, and started walking over.

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
story:
Michael sat cross-legged on the rug in Dev's basement, balancing the laptop on a stack of old board games. The screen glowed in the dim room, and somewhere behind the water heater a fan hummed steadily. He had typed a heading, "Dev's Comics Reviews," in big letters at the top of his very first web page, and now the words sat stubbornly against the left edge.

"I want it in the middle," Michael said. "Exactly the middle."

"Then you need CSS," said Dev, who was sprawled on the couch with a comic open on his chest, only half watching. "Add a style. There's a thing called text-align."

Michael tried it, typing text-align: center into the style for his heading, and hit refresh. The words slid to the middle of the page, right where he wanted them. That should have been the end of it, but a question snagged him. The middle of what? Before, the letters had hugged the left side, so how did the page know how far to move them? He stared at the heading and tried to imagine invisible measurements underneath it.

"Wait," he said slowly. "When it was left-aligned, the text only took up this much space." He held his thumb and finger a few inches apart. "But to find the middle, something has to know the whole width. The letters aren't that wide."

Dev set his comic down. "Try an experiment. You're the scientist type anyway."

Michael retrieved a small notebook from his backpack and wrote the word MIDDLE, then an approximate sketch of the page with the heading drawn in. He had an idea. If the heading itself stretched all the way across, then centering the text would land it in the middle of the page. If the heading were only as wide as its words, the text would sit off to one side. He gave the heading a temporary background color, a garish green, and refreshed again.

The green bar ran from the left edge of the page to the right edge, the whole width, with the centered words floating in the middle of it. Michael laughed out loud. "It's a block element. It stretches across the full width of its container. That's why the text lands in the middle of the page when I center it." Dev leaned over the couch arm to look, nodded once, and went back to his comic.

Michael removed the green background and saved the file. The heading sat clean and centered, exactly where he had wanted it, and beneath it he began typing the first line of Dev's first review. "Start with issue number one," Dev said without looking up. Michael's fingers were already moving.
